title: Infertility
intro: Infertility means not becoming pregnant after a year of regular unprotected intercourse. It affects many couples and may be caused by factors in the woman, the man or both, and sometimes no cause is found. Many couples succeed with time, advice or medical treatment. Support is available for the emotional strain.

sections.heading: How common and what causes it
paragraphs: About one in six couples has difficulty conceiving. In women, causes include ovulation problems such as polycystic ovary syndrome, blocked fallopian tubes, endometriosis, fibroids and age-related decline in egg quality. In men, low sperm count, poor sperm movement or shape and blockages may play a role. Smoking, heavy drinking, obesity and some illnesses and medicines reduce fertility.

sections.heading: Age and timing
paragraphs: Female fertility declines with age, especially after about 35. Male fertility also decreases gradually. Having sex every two to three days throughout the cycle works as well as trying to time ovulation, and avoids stress.

sections.heading: Investigations
paragraphs: Doctors look at both partners. For women this includes hormone tests, ultrasound, and checking whether tubes are open. For men, a semen analysis is the key test. Help is usually offered after a year of trying, or sooner if the woman is over 35 or there are known problems.

sections.heading: Treatment options
paragraphs: Treatment depends on the cause. Lifestyle changes, ovulation-inducing medicines, treatment of underlying conditions or surgery may help. Intrauterine insemination places prepared sperm inside the womb. In vitro fertilisation combines eggs and sperm in the laboratory and transfers an embryo to the womb. ICSI injects a single sperm into an egg and is used mainly for male factor problems.

These treatments involve hormone medicine, repeated visits, costs and a chance of multiple pregnancy. Success rates depend on age, the cause and number of attempts, and many couples need more than one cycle. Rules about funding differ between countries and insurers.

sections.heading: Coping emotionally
paragraphs: Infertility can cause grief, stress and strain on relationships. Counselling, support groups and honest conversations help. It is acceptable to take breaks or to stop treatment. Other options such as adoption or living child-free can be considered.

examples.title: Preparing for a first visit
examples.text: Imagine you have tried for a year without success. You could both write down cycle details, medical history and medicines, and ask for tests for both partners rather than assuming the cause lies with one.

examples.title: Deciding on treatment
examples.text: Suppose your doctor suggests IVF. You might ask about success chances for your age, risks, costs and what the alternatives are, and set a limit for how many cycles you want to try.
